card: Queen of Bellflower · Queen of Cups
notes: The plate's downturned bell (sheds rain, still rings) is the load-bearing image in every field. Second reversal (care with a ledger) is the risky one — check it doesn't read as diagnosis.

readingLine: Deep water with a level surface — that's the trick of her, and it costs more than it shows. You've been holding weather for other people this week. The bell of the flower faces down, note, so it can ring and still shed rain.

The harbor everyone rows to. She listens the way a bay receives boats — nothing capsizes, everything docks. Worth noticing who plays her in your week, and whether it's been you for longer than anyone asked out loud, or thought to check.
question: Whose weather did you carry this week, and where is it stored?
Who checks the water level of the person doing the holding?
libraryEntry: Court cards are job descriptions, and hers is the hardest in the suit: keeper of other people's water. The Queen of Bellflower is who people mean when they say they just needed somewhere to put a hard week — the level voice, the unhurried tea, the sense of a harbor with room left. The plate hangs her flower face-down, which is accurate botany and better psychology: a bell in that position sheds rain and still rings. Receiving without flooding is a skill, and she has it. The card's standing question is about maintenance. Harbors silt up. The person who absorbs everyone's storms acquires a sea floor of sediment nobody ever asks about, least of all her. Drawn in a daily reading, she tends to mean one of two people: someone holding you, who deserves more than being treated as infrastructure — or you, holding the room, overdue for an honest sounding of what's accumulated under all that competent calm.

Every suit has a card that other people experience more than the person holding it, and this is Bellflower's. Her gift is capacity: the friend who asks the second question, the colleague who notices the door close a little differently, the one adult in the kitchen at the hard family dinner. Depth is her medium the way soil is the gardener's. The engraving hangs the bellflower face-down on purpose — open enough to receive, angled enough not to fill with every passing rain. That angle is the whole curriculum. People who hold others well are often assumed to be bottomless, mostly because they never mention otherwise. The assumption is convenient for everyone standing in the rain. The card, drawn today, is usually an inventory prompt. Either there's a queen in your week who has been quietly load-bearing — worth naming, worth thanking in words. Or the queen is you, and the harbor's own weather report is several seasons overdue.
altText: Engraved plate: a full open bloom sigil above the suit's downturned bellflower mark.
Queen's plate: six-petaled bloom over a hanging bell, slate stamp, double hairline border.
reversedReadingLine: The harbor, silted. Reversed, the holding has gone automatic — the nods arrive on time, the tea appears, and somewhere behind the level voice nobody is home. If the queen here is you, expect to be the last to notice; the performance fools its performer longest.

A bell filled to the brim — one more rain and it pours on whoever stands closest. Held feelings have a capacity line, unmarked but real, and your week may be near it. Spilling scheduled beats spilling surprise, as any harbor master can confirm.
reversedQuestion: Where has your care gone automatic, and what would refill it?
What have you absorbed lately that was never yours to keep?
reversedLibraryEntry: Reversed, the queen's craft curdles in one of two directions, and the first is depletion. The harbor stayed open every day for years; dredging was never scheduled; now the level voice runs on procedure. She still asks the second question but no longer hears the answer, and the tea is a stall. People in this state are usually the last to know — you would be too — partly because their entire reputation is being fine, and reputations that useful get defended by everyone nearby. The bellflower on the plate droops a few degrees past its healthy hang — the difference between shedding rain and simply pointing at the ground. What tips it back upright is rarely dramatic rest, which such people are bad at anyway. It's reciprocity: one person who asks her the second question and sits still for the answer. Capacity, it turns out, was never bottomless. It was replenished, invisibly, back when someone else was also holding a corner of the sky.

The second reversal is stranger: holding as holding-on. Depth can be used the way moats are — genuinely deep water, deployed for keeping. Reversed this way, the queen's care develops a ledger. Confidences are kept, and counted. Support arrives, with terms accruing silently. The one adult in the kitchen starts to require that the kitchen never quite grow up, since being needed has become the pay. None of this announces itself from inside; it feels like devotion meeting insufficient gratitude, which is the tell. Real harbors let boats leave. That's most of what makes them harbors rather than nets, and the bellflower's open mouth — the plate insists on it — points down and outward, spilling forward, holding nothing back for leverage. Drawn reversed on a day this rings true, the card asks for an honest audit of one of your relationships' currents: who docks, who departs freely, and what, precisely, is charged at the mooring.
